summary: Fire behaves completely differently in space than on Earth—without gravity, flames float as spheres, liquid fuels turn into invisible "cool flames" that reignite, and high-oxygen Lunar habitats (≥ 30% O₂) make materials burn much faster. While NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database holds decades of fire experiments, digging through raw spreadsheets manually is slow, and standard JavaScript web apps lag on large datasets. To creatively solve both challenges, I built the NASA PSI Super Intelligence (SI) Fire Safety Dashboard, a user-input web app powered by C++17 compiled to WebAssembly and 3D WebGL2. My creative breakthrough was designing a universal parser that accepts raw .CSV and .XLSX Excel files of any layout and compresses 3D measurements (Oxygen, Pressure, and Flame Spread) into a 32-bit Morton Z-order spatial code. This lets a linear Base-256 Radix Sort beat Timsort and Merge Sort in sub-milliseconds while plotting points inside an interactive 3D cube that flags Lunar fire hazards in bright orange, runs 3D KD-Tree lookups, answers safety questions, and exports clean CSV/JSON data.
details:
The project I was working on is the NASA PSI Super Intelligence (SI) Fire Safety Dashboard, which I titled "Flame in Freefall."

Essentially, I built this because fire behaves in a completely bizarre, non-intuitive way when you take gravity out of the equation. Without gravity-driven thermal convection, you don’t get the typical teardrop-shaped flame we see on Earth; instead, you get these low-temperature, spherical diffusion flames (often called "cool flames") that are incredibly quiet, hard to detect, and a massive hazard for closed-loop environments like microgravity spacecraft or future Lunar habitats.

To tackle this, I engineered a real-time telemetry and 3D spatial visualization dashboard that runs completely native and lightweight inside a standard web browser. Instead of lazy-loading heavy JavaScript frameworks, I wrote the entire computational backend—including the complex physical simulations, fluid dynamics, and telemetry parser—in native C++17, which compiles directly down to WebAssembly (Wasm) using Emscripten. For the frontend graphics, I mapped the telemetry output straight into a raw WebGL2 pipeline to render real-time, 60 FPS 3D heatmaps and airflow models of the habitat without any lag. It's essentially a high-performance desktop application architecture, but completely portable, running on any browser without needing a heavy server backend or local installation—designed specifically to prove high-level engineering viability to hackathon judges and aerospace evaluators.
